item.title: A microfluidic fluorescence lifetime screening platform bridges in vitro and in vivo formats and enables discovery of Amyloid β aggregation inhibitors
item.description:
Súil Collins, Liisa D. van Vliet, Fabrice Gielen, Matej Janeček, Nino F. Läubli, Sara Wagner Valladolid, Chetan Poudel, Ana Fernandez-Villegas, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78202-8
Abstract Inhibiting the aggregation of Amyloid β (1-42) is a promising strategy for the development of disease-modifying Alzheimer’s disease therapeutics. To date, however, no sufficiently efficacious inhibitors have been identified, despite the best efforts of more than 200 advanced drug development campaigns. This failure can be partially attributed to limitations in current in vitro compound screening and in vivo validation assays. Here, we report a high throughput assay platform based on the use of a fluorescence lifetime aggregation sensor that can be applied in vitro and in vivo. This microfluidic “nanoFLIM” assay presents a cost-effective and reliable alternative to conventional early-stage small molecule discovery platforms for cell-free Amyloid β aggregation. The fluorescence lifetime sensor can dynamically monitor peptide aggregation in cellular and Caenorhabditis elegans disease models, providing directly comparable aggregation kinetics, which is not achievable by any other method. The power of this unified platform for accelerating hit-to-lead strategies, lowering attrition rates and expediting in vivo screening, was demonstrated with a pilot screening campaign of 445 compounds, revealing an inhibitor that can inhibit Amyloid β self-assembly both in vitro as well as in cellular and whole organism disease models.

item.title: AS01E-adjuvanted RSV pre-F protein vaccine in adults with lung or kidney transplant: a phase 2b randomized trial
item.description:
Catherine Small, Deepali Kumar, Anum Abbas, Ana Sánchez Fructuoso, Shigeyoshi Yamanaga, Virginia Luz Pérez González, Hristos Karakizlis, Michael Nissen, et al.
Nature Communications, vol. 17, issue 1
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78584-9
Abstract Immunocompromised adults are at increased risk of severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease. This multicountry, open-label phase 2b trial (NCT05921903) evaluated the immunogenicity and safety of the AS01 E -adjuvanted RSV prefusion F protein vaccine (adjuvanted RSVPreF3) over 12 months in kidney or lung transplant recipients ≥18 years, randomized 1:1 to receive one ( n = 131) or two doses 30–60 days apart ( n = 130). A control group of non-immunocompromised adults ≥50 years ( n = 125) received a single dose. The primary outcome was the mean geometric increase in RSV-A and RSV-B neutralizing titers one month following a second adjuvanted RSVPreF3 dose relative to the first dose in transplant recipients. Secondary outcomes included assessment of the safety and immunogenicity of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 in transplant recipients compared with the control group. In transplant recipients receiving two doses, neutralizing titers against RSV-A and RSV-B were numerically higher one month post-dose 2 than post-dose 1 (mean geometric increases: 1.34 [95% CI: 1.20, 1.48] for RSV-A [ n = 111] and 1.26 [95% CI: 1.14, 1.40] for RSV-B [ n = 111]). A single dose was immunogenic in transplant recipients, but showed slower and generally lower initial neutralizing responses than in non-immunocompromised controls, specifically in individuals receiving mycophenolate. RSVPreF3-specific CD4 + T-cell frequencies increased after vaccination versus baseline in all groups. Humoral and cell-mediated immune responses remained above baseline for 12 months post-vaccination. Both doses of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 were well tolerated and had a similar and acceptable safety profile. Overall, these results support a favorable benefit-risk profile of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 in kidney and lung transplant recipients.

item.title: Percolation and site energy distribution jointly control Li+ transport in disordered rocksalt positive electrodes
item.description:
Junhong Liao, Zihui Li, Hao Chen, Yaoshu Xie, Ziyi Man, Shendong Tan, Yiyang Qu, Shixi Zhao, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79420-w
Abstract Disordered rocksalt positive electrodes are promising candidates for high-energy batteries, yet their ion transport kinetics is constrained by an incomplete understanding of Li transport in disordered environments. Conventional percolation theory focuses on topological connectivity but often overlooks the critical role of the energy landscape. Here, leveraging actively fine-tuned machine learning interatomic potentials combined with experimental validation, we quantitatively resolve the interplay between Li percolation connectivity and the Li-site energy distribution. We reveal a trade-off whereby increasing cation disorder enhances topological connectivity but concurrently broadens the site energy distribution, inducing a rugged energy landscape that suppresses overall diffusion. To reconcile these conflicting factors, we construct a design map spanning the full Li–Mn–Ti–O composition space, establishing a Li-site energy rectified percolation metric that transforms their interaction into a quantifiable descriptor. This framework enables the identification of Li 1.3 Mn 0.4 Ti 0.3 O 2 , which delivers a specific capacity of 294 mAh g −1 . Furthermore, we demonstrate that inducing a phase transition toward a partially disordered spinel-like state simultaneously enhances percolation connectivity and narrows the energy landscape, achieving a specific capacity of 316 mAh g −1 . This work provides insights into the ion transport mechanisms in disordered electrode materials and offers practical design principles for battery systems.

item.title: Non-equilibrium resonance scattering in intramolecular charge transport drives conformational changes
item.description:
YoungJu Park, Taegil Kim, Jonghyeok Baek, Seongbin Park, Daeho Kim, ChaeHo Shin, Sokhuoy Sam, Wonyoung Kim, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79555-w
Abstract Intramolecular charge transport is conventionally described as proceeding along a static ground-state potential, with the carrier acting as a passive probe of a fixed electronic landscape. Here, using alkanethiolate-based molecular junctions, we show that the carrier itself can drive conformational reorganization once the applied bias brings backbone-delocalized molecular orbitals into the transmission window. Combined electrical and in situ structural measurements resolve a threshold-activated transition to a gauche-defect state coincident with the onset of orbital-mediated transport. We rationalize this coupling through a quantum resonance scattering framework in which accessible orbitals act as scattering potentials that transiently host the injected charge, depositing energy into nuclear motion with an efficiency set by molecule–electrode coupling and Franck–Condon overlap. The framework quantitatively reproduces the measured response and predicts the enhanced behavior of amide-containing junctions. Together, these results suggest that charge-transport–structure feedback can be understood in terms of microscopic parameters governing resonance-mediated energy transfer, and that these parameters may be tuned through chemical design.

item.title: Sugar rationing during the first 1000 days of life and biological aging and age-related diseases
item.description:
Yuelan Gao, Jun Yu, Jianming Xu, Yuzhou Zhang, Haoyu Chen, Mary Ho, Ka Wai Kam, Alvin L. Young, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79639-7
Abstract Early-life nutritional conditions may influence biological aging and age-related health, but the long-term associations of early exposure to sugar rationing remain unclear. Here we investigate the associations of early-life exposure to sugar rationing with biological aging and age-related diseases among 54,201 participants in the UK Biobank, taking advantage of the abrupt end of post-war sugar rationing as a natural experiment. Exposure to sugar rationing during the first 1000 days of life is associated with lower biological age acceleration, with stronger associations observed among participants with longer exposure durations. The association is more pronounced in females and remains consistent across strata of genetic susceptibility. Early-life exposure to sugar rationing is also associated with lower risks of age-related cataract and chronic kidney disease, but not with several other age-related diseases examined. Overall, these findings suggest that early-life exposure to a population-level nutritional policy is associated with biological aging and several age-related diseases in later life, highlighting the potential long-term relevance of early-life nutritional environments for healthy aging.

item.title: Directional motility of crystallizing cholesterol on supported lipid bilayers
item.description:
Hyunhyuk Tae, Younghwan Choe, Dongping Jiang, Lepakshi Gnanasekaran, Soohyun Park, Ji-Yu Zhu, Guillermo C. Bazan, Vladimir P. Zhdanov, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79445-1
Abstract Cholesterol crystallization within phospholipid bilayers necessarily remodels the surrounding membrane, creating dynamic feedback between growing crystallites and locally changing membrane. Using fluorescence microscopy, we show that lipid-coated, cholesterol-rich crystallites self-propel on the bilayer surface along directional trajectories, including circular, unidirectional, and reciprocating motion. We hypothesize that crystallite motilities arise from local cholesterol depletion in the underlying bilayer, generating gradients in composition, rigidity, and thus adhesion, which induce directional forces analogous to those involved in haptotaxis and/or durotaxis. Fluorescence lifetime imaging with a mechanosensitive probe reveals time-resolved changes in membrane packing, consistent with this mechanism. Single particle tracking and mathematical modeling support the mechanical plausibility of a working model in which crystallization-induced cholesterol redistribution may generate dynamic rigidity gradients at crystallite–membrane interface. Tuning membrane states yields a quantitative operating map that relates composition to motility, providing model-dependent design guidance for controlling cholesterol crystallite transport on lipid interfaces.

item.title: Co-administration of the long-acting monoclonal antibody AZD7442 and bivalent Ancestral/BA.1 vaccination is well-tolerated in immunosuppressed patients highly vulnerable to infection with SARS-CoV-2 virus: the results of the multicentre, open-label, phase II randomised controlled, RAPID-PROTECTION trial
item.description:
Nicole Frumento, Catharine Porter, Joanne Euden, Melanie Varley, Lawrence Raisanen, Richard Adams, Craig Bodman, Miles Carroll, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78637-z
Abstract Immunocompromised individuals remain at risk of severe COVID-19. This multicentre, open-label, phase II randomised controlled trial evaluated the safety, pharmacokinetics and immunogenicity of co-administering the long-acting monoclonal antibody AZD7442 with a bivalent (Ancestral/BA.1) mRNA/LNP SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. A total of 139 immunocompromised adults received AZD7442 followed 28 days later by vaccination. AZD7442 was well tolerated, with no serious adverse events. Serum AZD7442 concentrations peaked at day 28 and remained detectable across disease cohorts at day 180. Anti-Spike antibody responses increased after AZD7442 and reached their highest levels after vaccination. Although binding antibodies against Omicron variants increased post-vaccination, neutralisation of Omicron remained limited after both AZD7442 and vaccination. Vaccination preferentially boosted antibodies targeting S2, the S1 N-terminal domain and receptor-binding domain epitopes not bound by AZD7442, and increased S2-specific memory B cells. Vaccine-induced T-cell responses were cross-reactive between ancestral and Omicron variants. Our findings support consideration of combined antibody and vaccine strategies in future therapeutic antibody development. The trial is registered with the International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial Number registry (ISRCTN53507177).

item.title: Humanized yeast ORC drives R-loop dependent transcription-replication conflicts and global gene dysregulation
item.description:
Clare S. K. Lee, Maxime Lalonde, Tobias Straub, Myriam Zheng, Elizabeth Márquez-Gómez, Melina Riepl, Bozhao Dong, Ioannis Tsirkas, et al.
Nature Communications, vol. 17, issue 1
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79167-4
Abstract The Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) recruits Mini-Chromosome Maintenance (MCM) hexamers to initiate eukaryotic DNA replication. While yeast ORC binds specific DNA motifs, human ORC binds sequence-agnostically nucleosome-depleted promoter regions. Here, using a mutant yeast model that recapitulates the human ORC binding landscape, we demonstrate that pervasive and unscheduled ORC binding at promoters in the compact yeast genome generates R-loop associated transcription-replication conflicts and disrupts gene expression across thousands of genes. Unexpectedly, we also uncover that substituting endogenous gene promoters with a replication origin sequence maintains robust transcription. We reveal that this intrinsic, promoter-like function relies on the ability of origins to form a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) encoded within the origin’s sequence composition. However, origin-substituted loci reposition the +1 nucleosome which drives the transcription machinery to select alternative transcription start sites (TSSs). Thus, origins and promoters share an intrinsic chromatin structure-controlled ability to drive transcription initiation. Together, our results show that origin licensing in compact genomes relies on sequence-specific, coupled origin licensing to insulate transcription from the replication machinery.
